chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ibn Abi Nasr from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Abu al-Abbas from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who pledged two slaves to another, and one of them died; would his right be in the other? He said, 'Yes.' I said, or a house that burned down; would his right be in the ashes/ground? He said, 'Yes.' Or two beasts, would his right be in one of them? He said, 'Yes.' Or goods that spoil due to the length of time they were left, or food that spoils, or a slave who contracted smallpox and went blind, or clothes that were left folded and not aired until they perished? He said, 'This is permissible to take; his right remains upon him.'

And I asked him how the pledge remains with what is in it if it is an animal or beast or gold or silver or goods, and a calamity befalls it—fire or thieves—and all his property perishes, except that part, and some of his goods have perished, and he has no proof of his loss? He said, 'If all his goods are gone and nothing is found for him, then there is nothing upon him.' And he said, 'If part of his property is gone and he still has property, he is not believed [to claim total loss], and it is ruled for every pledge that has produce/yield, that its yield is calculated for the owner of the pledge from what is upon him.'

key_terms.رَهْن: Collateral or pledge given to secure a debt
key_terms.عَبْدَيْنِ: Two slaves (common form of property in classical fiqh)
key_terms.غَلَّةٌ: Yield, produce, or benefit derived from the pledge

ai.seo_question: What happens to the debt if the pledged collateral is destroyed or lost?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *ghalla* (yield/profit) in *rahn* (collateral), establishing that the creditor bears the risk of loss for the pledged asset while in their possession, yet the debtor remains liable for the debt value. It distinguishes between total loss without proof, which discharges the debtor, and partial loss, where the remaining collateral's yield offsets the debt, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on equitable risk distribution in commercial contracts. This ruling underscores the practical application of risk allocation in pre-modern Islamic markets, ensuring creditors do not unjustly enrich themselves from the debtor's loss while maintaining the debtor's ultimate financial responsibility.
